question: What story about humanity do your daily actions tell?
Close your eyes and scan your body. Notice where you are holding tension or stiffness. Breathe deeply and slow down. What is your body asking to do and what does it need right now?
What game are you playing that you never consciously chose to enter?
If I want to feel that I have enough right now, what do I need to stop doing or let go?
Consistency cannot be guaranteed, but you can create the conditions to make it more likely. Before you try to become a more disciplined person, how are you creating a more disciplined environment?

A two-part question for today:

Where am I rushing right now when I should be moving deliberately?

Where am I dragging my feet right now when I should be moving fast?
What are you doing today that will benefit you in a decade?

I recently asked a friend if he wanted to hit a certain business milestone and he said, “That depends. What does it cost me?”

Writing down your goals is easy. Everybody wants the glamorous result. What really matters is whether you want the costs associated with it: the money, the time, the tradeoffs.

Don't merely ask yourself what do I want to achieve, but also what am I willing to pay?

If you want a plant to grow, you can fuss over it every day—watering, weeding, moving it toward the sun. Or you can place it in the right soil and let nature do most of the work. A seed planted in the right spot often thrives on its own. Life is much the same. Progress is not only about how hard you work, but also about where you decide to work.

Where is your energy better spent right now: pushing harder or planting yourself in better ground?
A question from ​Christopher Celeste​, “If I were to ask you to name what you love most in life, how long would it take to name yourself?”
Who are you afraid of disappointing and how would your choices change if you released that fear?
Many of the good things in life are downstream from being helpful and useful to others. What can you do today to be useful to someone else?
What looks like consistency and commitment can sometimes be fear in disguise. Are you sticking with it because it still serves you or because it's what you already know?
Let's say the worst-case scenario actually occurs. There are obviously things you won't like about it. But what aspects of that scenario are you excited about?
Which belief once protected you, but now confines you?

It is common to think about what you would like to accomplish. It is less common to think about what must be discarded to make space for your new endeavors. The time must come from somewhere. What do you need to give up to make space for what you would like to achieve?
If your partner or close friend could change one habit of yours, what would they choose — and why might they be right?

Life is always progressing to the next stage. As you enter a new season, habits that previously served you well may need to be refreshed or adjusted. Which one of your current habits have you outgrown and is in need of a change?
What unfinished task is still hogging your mental real estate and needs to be let go?
What aspect of your work is hardest to copy? How can you amplify it?

There's a difference between feeling tired and feeling empty. One probably needs sleep. The other may need purpose.

Are you low on rest or low on meaning?

Your environment whispers suggestions all day long—eat this, click that, sit here. Look around you right now. What small change could you make to your surroundings that would steer you toward good habits and away from distractions?

Each person carries an invisible backpack full of unfinished tasks. These things can weigh on you, especially the ones that you feel like you should do but know you probably won't make time for.

There are two ways to lighten the load: finish the task or let it go. Give yourself permission to stop worrying about the things you're never going to do.

What's weighing down your backpack that needs to be released?

Timing influences communication.

Talk about potential mistakes before they happen and people start looking for ways to prevent them.

Talk about actual mistakes after they happen and people start looking for reasons to defend their actions.

What do we need to be talking about now, so we can learn the lessons before we need them?

I'm usually asleep from 5am to 6am, but when I wake up early I tend to enjoy it. Start the day slow. Watch the sunrise. Get a few things done before everyone else wakes up.

Meanwhile, I am often awake from 10pm to 11pm and I find that I tend to use the time poorly. Passively watching TV or scrolling on a screen. Late night snacking. Overthinking things that are unimportant.

Trading the last hour of the night for the first hour in the morning would be a pretty high value trade for me.

Which hours of your day tend to return the most value and which ones tend to return the least?

A question inspired by ​The Simple Path to Wealth​:

Which single expense in your life delivers the least happiness per dollar and which delivers the most happiness per dollar?

The cost of convenience is vitality. You can have a lot of things done for you in the modern world — and many of them are great time savers! — but the feeling of being alive comes from being fully engaged in the right task, not free from all tasks.

Sure, you can automate and delegate all sorts of things, but the more interesting question is, “What fills you with so much liveliness that you want to do the work yourself?”

A question from ​The Strategy Deck​ by Seth Godin:

“Better waves make better surfers. Are you on the right beach?”
Look at all the good around you. Of all the lives you could have lived, how wonderful and special is it that you get to live this one?
Which relationships in your life push you toward growth, and which reinforce stagnation?
What is something you deeply believe but rarely live out?
What hard lesson keeps repeating itself in your life because you refuse to learn it?
If a competent CEO got to run your life for a day, what is the first thing they would eliminate?
Who do you secretly envy—and what does that reveal about what you truly value?
Which distractions in your life have become disguised as priorities?
Is your default setting to defend your limitations or expand your possibilities?
What single habit, if implemented consistently for the rest of this year, would transform your life the most?

You get to pick a new career based on one factor: Your job is to do the activity that most frequently puts you into a flow state.

Flow state = you feel fully immersed in your work, you're in “the zone,” time flies by without you realizing it, etc.

What do you choose?

A question from entrepreneur Nathan Barry on patience:

“When does it benefit me to be patient and when does it not?”

Instead of running from parts of your life and compensating elsewhere, what if you began to restore what is broken?

(​​Share this on X​​)

It's hard to get a great outcome when your resources — time, money, attention — are spread thin. Are you concentrating your energies on a small set of targets?

(​​Share this on X​​)

A question from ​Nick Cammarata​ to inspire action:

“If I had 10x the agency I have, what would I do?”

What is one topic you are so fascinated by that you could teach a class about it?

(​​Share this on X​​)

What do I need to let go of this year to create space for what I really want?

(​​Share this on X​​)

Cheaper, faster, or better?

(​​Share this on X​​)

Bad things are always happening loudly: the injury, the flat tire, the mistake that gets you criticized. Everybody talks about the moments that make things a hassle.

Good things are always happening quietly: the completed workout, the healthy meal, the ten minutes of writing. Nobody talks about the little moments that add up.

What good things have you done quietly today?

Habits need to be revised from time to time. Which habits have become more important and you need to double down on next year? Which habits are no longer serving you and need to be replaced next year?

(​​Share this on X​​)

What is one lesson you have learned this year?

(​​Share this on X​​)

How does this action feed the next? How does this project make the next project easier?

(​​Share this on X​​)

The common narrative is that kids learn faster than adults, but if you watch any toddler they spend a large portion of the day attempting things that are on the edge of their ability.

How much time have you spent on the edge of your ability today?

The best way to handle pressure is to apply it.

What if you played the game like you were always on offense?

(​​Share this on X​​)

We undervalue health if we have not recently experienced illness.

We undervalue wealth if we have not recently experienced poverty.

We undervalue kindness if we have not recently experienced cruelty.

What might you be undervaluing right now?

(​Share this on X​)

Where has your mind been focused recently? Are you primarily thinking about your past, your present, or your future? How does focusing on a different timeframe change your thoughts?

(​​Share this on X​​)

What project are you still working on that has already peaked? Is it time to let it go and begin climbing the next mountain?

(​Share this on X​)

Think about someone who has the results you want or a lifestyle you admire. It's easy to want the results. What are the costs and tradeoffs of their lifestyle that you may be overlooking?

(​Share this on X​)

Forget about the outcome and focus on what precedes it.

Am I putting myself in good positions and creating the conditions for success?

(​Share this on X​)
When you woke up this morning, did you expect today to have many joys or many frustrations?
A thoughtful question from author Morgan Housel: “What was true a generation ago that no longer is, and who is clinging to that old truth?”
Ask yourself this question three times and try to refine and improve your answer each time: What do I really want?
A four-pack on love:
What weight are you carrying unnecessarily?

Exploration is how you discover what works.

Persistence is how you make the most of what already works.

What does your situation require? More exploration or more persistence?

(​Share this on Twitter​)

Many things in life go through phases. It can be like the seasons: spring, summer, fall, winter. Each season has its own set of needs and demands.

Think about something important to you. Maybe it's a project or a job. Perhaps a hobby or even a relationship. What season are you in right now and what does that season require?
When are you seized by the thrill of what you are trying to accomplish?
What can I do today to practice five minutes of self-care?
Which activities are the best expression of you? Can you spend five minutes doing one of them today?
Author and investor Morgan Housel shares a thought-provoking question: “Whose life do I admire that is secretly miserable?”
What conversation will you be proud of yourself for having even if it doesn't end with the outcome you want? Go have that conversation.
In many cases, the real talent is being obsessed with the thing. What are you willing to focus on so wholeheartedly that you are happy to ignore nearly everything else?

It's important to have boundaries in life, but sometimes you may feel guilty for enforcing them. Aren't I supposed to be generous? Am I unkind if I say no to this?

The question isn't whether to be flexible or firm, but when to be each one. A good life has a healthy mix of selfish boundaries and unselfish giving. You don't have to be all things at all times. Sometimes you pour for others and sometimes you refill your own cup.

What does this moment call for?

What is in the way of what I want?

Can I come up with at least three different paths around it?

Instead of asking, “What would make me feel happy?” try asking, “What would make the group excited?”

Many of the best moments in life happen when the group is having fun. You feed off one another's energy. What can you do to laugh or gasp or scream or smile with others?

A wonderful question from ​Morgan Housel​ on measuring your results internally rather than externally:

“Would I be happy with this result if no one other than me and my family could see it, and I didn't compare the result to the appearance of other people's success?”
How do you want to feel at the end of today? What do you need to do now, so you can feel this way?

How can I overlap the things I enjoy?

For example, maybe you want to exercise and spend time with your spouse. What type of exercise sounds fun to do with your spouse?

Or perhaps you'd like to hang out with friends and build your career. How can you find ways to work with people you like being around?

It doesn't always work, but there are usually a few areas of life you can overlap in an enjoyable way. Look for the overlap.

How should you measure your days? It's easy to measure your days in dollars earned or tasks completed, but there are other units of measurement to consider:

What unit of measurement serves you best right now?

What are you often silently complaining about in your head and who is the person you need to actually discuss your frustrations with?

People can't react to your thoughts, only your actions. Time spent complaining to yourself is often better spent selling someone else on a new way of doing things.

What is something you would be proud to fail on, if you had the courage to attempt it?

(​Share this on Twitter​)

Take whatever you are trying to accomplish and ask, “How could this be as easy as possible?”

How could I make meditating each day as easy possible? How could I make showing appreciation to my partner as easy as possible? How could I make finding great investment opportunities as easy as possible? And so on.

You may be surprised how effective the easy version can be.
Unspoken boundaries often cause frustration. What is one area of your life where you would benefit from having clearer boundaries, but haven't voiced them yet?
Make a list of the people in your field who enjoy unfair advantages. How can you collaborate with them?

What lifestyle do you love 80% of the time?

No lifestyle is perfect 100% of the time. I love having a few days each year to relax on the beach—but I wouldn't want to do that every day, or even most days.

What lifestyle feels ideal for you most of the time? Cultivate that.

There are two ways to grow: by adding or by shedding.

Do you need to add something or do you need to shed something?
Is the situation actually complicated or is it really quite straightforward, but you're making it complicated because it requires a lot of courage to make the straightforward decision?
What is one commitment you are continuing to do out of inertia, but—if you had the courage to eliminate it—you would immediately benefit from discarding it?

A question from business coach Jeanne Torre:

“Is that assumed or confirmed?”

Imagine your life as a book. What title would you give to the current chapter, and what is going to be the next?

(​Thanks to Jard​ for today's question.)
What is something you want, but you haven't asked for?
When have I felt most joyful this year and what steps can I take to recreate those conditions?
Design for relaxation. What is one change I can make to my environment that promotes mental peace and reduces stress?
What if you stopped looking for new ideas and simply focused on the best idea you have right now?

Imagine there is a small version of you and a big version.

When you are playing small, your behavior is timid, you feel less than, and you are often surrounded by people and projects that drain you.

When you are playing big, your behavior is confident, you feel motivated, and you tend to be investing in people and projects that energize you.

How can you spend more time playing the big version of yourself this year?

Which responsibilities, relationships, or projects have been weighing heavily on me and can I give myself permission to let one of them go right now?

(​Share this on Twitter​)
Think about something you have been trying to make progress on recently. What is a completely different line of attack for solving it or a wildly different approach you can explore?

Slow down for a minute. Close your eyes. Scan your body.

Where are you holding tension right now?

Take a deep breath. Relax.

Artist and educator Corita Kent had a set of rules she often shared with her students. One of them read, “There is no win and no fail. There is only make.”

What are you making today?

Winston Churchill once said, “It is not enough that we do our best; sometimes we must do what is required.”

Think about what you are working toward this year. Are you doing what is required or are you looking for a shortcut?
Who are you trying to become this year? Which actions will reinforce that identity?

Who is one person you want to spend more time around next year?

(​Share this on Twitter​)
What worked well this year and is worth doubling down on in 2024?
What are my favorite hours of the day and what adjustments can I make to ensure they are under my control?

This question comes from a reader named Mac, who shared ​this story​ with me:

“My dad and I love basketball. We used to play hoops in the front yard almost every day when I was growing up. He was also my coach for many years.

One thing that always stuck with me was him saying “shoot to make it.” I think there's a lot of moments in basketball and in life where we are just “throwing a shot up” and hoping it goes in.

How I interpreted his mantra was to have intention. If you are going to take a shot, take a good one and take it to make it. I always come back to what he said when I'm evaluating decisions I'm making and actions I take.

Am I shooting to make it?”

Challenge yourself to do something out of your normal routine. What is one thing you can do this week that is different than what you do on a normal week?

(​Share this on Twitter​)

Half your problems are just your mind making minor things seem like major things.

What are you over-emphasizing right now?

It's remarkable how uncomplicated it is most of the time. The hard part is not knowing what to do, but having the resolve to do it. What is one thing you know you should do right now and you just need to step up and do it?

(​Share this on Twitter​)

Opportunities in life come through people. Who do you need to connect with to gain access to the opportunities you want?

(​Share this on Twitter​)
Which of your current habits is least aligned with the type of person you hope to become?

Think of your childhood. What is one area where your parents did a good job? What is one area where they could have done better?

(​Share this on Twitter​)

In your professional life, who do you admire most?

In your personal life, who do you admire most?

Look back ten years and you can probably identify a few blind spots or mistaken beliefs you held at the time. Now, fast forward ten years from today… what are likely to be your current blind spots? What are you not spending enough time thinking about or perhaps even willfully ignoring?
How can the work you're doing today accumulate and layer on top of what you did yesterday? Find ways to compound your efforts.

Imagine you are at the end of your life and you are granted the ability to repeat one day. Which period of your life do you choose to repeat? Which phase of life would you want to go back to? Does that tell you anything about how you should be spending your time today?

Think about something you are facing right now. Have you been trying to think your way to a solution or act your way to a solution? Sometimes you need more action, sometimes you need a better strategy.

Who do you still owe an apology? Can you make one in the next 5 minutes?

(​Share this on Twitter​)
What is the 2-minute version of the task I'm avoiding?

It's easy to gravitate toward the idea of having lots of friends, but you'll probably benefit more from strengthening your “inner circle” friendships than from simply gaining more friends.

Who belongs in your inner circle? Can you reach out to one of them right now?

Two questions at the center of improvement:

How quickly can you get started?

How quickly can you learn from your mistakes?

In what areas of your life do you communicate well?

In what areas do you communicate poorly?
What are the current habits that are hindering your future progress?

A simple question that can prevent a lot of future headaches:

What is not being said right now that needs to be said? What problems could we avoid in the future, if only we had the courage to talk about them now?

What is the one task that, if completed, will make today a success? What can you do to make it as easy as possible to get started?

(​Share this on Twitter​)
In which direction are your habits currently steering your life?
What small step can you take today that will put you on the path toward something wonderful?
It's easy to find ways to improve when you are genuinely curious about something. Rather than asking yourself, “How can I be better at this?” start by asking, “How can I be more curious about this?”

Think of a time you failed or struggled greatly.

If you were to view that experience in a more useful way, what story would you tell yourself? What did it teach you? How did it prepare you for what came next?

Turn your failures into lessons.
What is getting too much of my time right now? What is getting too little?
What is one activity you are naturally drawn to? Can you spend 5 minutes doing it today?
What is something that made you feel proud today? If nothing comes to mind, how can you spend the next 5 minutes in a way that will make you feel proud?

What is one habit you've formed that had a significant impact on your life?

(​See thousands of answers from my readers​.)
What are the current habits that are hindering your future progress?

If I do nothing, what will happen? If I act right now, what will happen?

Sometimes you need to let go. Sometimes you need to get going.

What's the one action that moves the needle more than 100 other actions? What's the one choice that renders 1000 other choices irrelevant?

Most things are not worth optimizing. Master the big moves and move quickly and peacefully through the other stuff.
When you're living a good day, what is one habit that tends to be part of that day? Can you find time for that habit today?
Apply the Pareto Principle to your relationships. Who are the few people that deliver the majority of happiness in your life? Can you schedule time with one of them today?
What's the most fun you could possibly have in one year?

What is one important lesson for life that isn't taught in school, but that you want to teach to your kids?

Today's question is a two-parter:

When I'm living a good day, what am I spending my time on?

Do the sources of information I am exposed to each day support that type of lifestyle or distract from it?
Does this habit still serve me or am I blindly following an old routine?
Is what I'm about to do today connected to what I'm going to value over the long-term?
What is the highest leverage activity you have ever done? Does that tell you anything about how to better spend your time?
This thing that I am unhappy about… is it actually hard to change or is it simply hard to have the courage to change it?
Where am I spending energy trying to please someone who actually doesn't care?
Is it better to delay getting started by weeks or months so I can be fully prepared? Or is it better to start right now with little to no preparation?
How would my daily schedule change if I did a little more of what I'm great at and a little less of what I'm not great at?
If you could spend 30 minutes today creating whatever you want, what would you create?
What has been the best hour of my week? How can I make it easier to have more hours like that?
What can I do today to improve by 1%?
Are the results I am expecting aligned with the habits I am following each day?

Eliminate. Focus. Close yourself to the world and ask, “What can I create today?”

Relax. Breathe. Open yourself to the world and ask, “What can I receive today?”

Imagine all your responsibilities and obligations vanish overnight.

What would you miss doing? What would you choose to add back to your life?

If you're searching for more time this year, start with a clean slate and choose what to add to your days rather than starting with a full schedule and trying to figure out what to eliminate.
It's one year from now. December 2023. The habit you were hoping to build during the year didn't stick. What is the most likely reason it failed?

How can I improve the energy of the situations I am involved in today?

You may not control the outcome, but you can influence it.

What is your relationship with self-discipline?

What is your relationship with self-forgiveness?

“When was a time in the past you successfully adapted and made a change?

What is a change you would benefit from making right now?”

There is one month left in the year. Most people are ready to coast to the finish line, but one good month can make the whole year feel like a success.

What can you do in the next 30 days to build momentum and finish the year on a high note?
How can I use the negative experiences in my life to drive me? What fuel can I draw from my failures? What lessons can I take from my grief? What insights can I extract from my embarrassments?
Do I need to spend more time searching for better information or do I need to spend more time acting on the information I already have? Is the bottleneck strategy or execution?
The question is not, “Will I succeed?” but rather, “What should I attempt?”
What do I need to accomplish today and how can I have the most fun possible while doing it?

What’s something good to “go a little overboard” on?

What's something you could benefit from caring less about?

Without altering the facts of the situation I am facing and without ignoring the reality of what must be done, what is the most useful and empowering story I can tell myself about what is happening and what I need to do next?

A (slightly modified) question from writer Nat Eliason on your consumption habits:

“What percentage of the media you consume on a daily basis was created in the last year? What percentage of the best and most useful information was created in the last year?”

A simple question to recalibrate the current situation:

“Aside from my thoughts, am I okay?”

The benefits that arise from a good relationship—whether it be in marriage, friendship, business, or otherwise—are often produced over a long time span.

Is it more important to win this battle or to maintain this relationship?

What is one previous habit I'd like to reclaim?

What is one current habit I'd like to let go?
What is one step I can take today to help create the outcomes I want in life?
Would you rather be right or be happy?

Sometimes it benefits us to be passive: to allow life to come to us and unfold without force.

Other times it benefits us to be aggressive: to bend the world to our will and actively shape the life we want.

Are you being too passive or too aggressive right now?
Is taking things so seriously improving my performance? How can today feel like play?

Here's a simple question to ask before jumping into “all the work” you have to do:

What will happen if I don't do this?

It's remarkable how many things can be eliminated from your to-do list.

What career would you realistically pursue if you wanted the most money?What career would you realistically pursue if you wanted the biggest impact?What career would you realistically pursue if you wanted to have the most fun?What career offers the best mix?

Instead of asking yourself, “What should I do first?”

Try asking, “What should I neglect first?”

Trim, edit, cull. Make space for better performance.
Who is someone you love spending time with, but you haven't seen recently? Can you reach out to them today?

A question from computer programmer Simon Sarris:

“If you have a ten year plan, what's stopping you from doing it in two?”

What type of work brings you the most happiness?

What type of work brings you the most meaning?

Are they the same or different?
What action can you take today that will contribute to something you will be proud of in 10 years?

Is this project pulling me in or am I pushing it forward? Is this relationship pulling me in or am I pushing it forward?

Some of my best outcomes arise when I double down on the things that are naturally pulling me in.

Think of the best coach, teacher, or leader you ever had. What can you learn from them?

Think of the worst coach, teacher, or leader you ever had. What can you learn from them?
Who (or what) do you need to forgive, so you can move on and live well?

The generalist becomes more powerful when they develop a specialty where they can apply their broad insight.

The specialist becomes more powerful when they develop a broader surface area of knowledge to connect with their expertise.

Which side are you favoring right now? Would you benefit from a broader area to apply your already honed skills? Or do you need deeper skills to unlock your general knowledge?

Sometimes we are too hard on ourselves and criticize our mistakes to an unhelpful degree. Sometimes we are too easy on ourselves and let excuses run our lives.

Which way are you leaning right now? How can you pull yourself back to center?
How, specifically, do you want your life to be better at this time next year?

What is an area you'd like to improve over the next decade?

How are you working toward that outcome today?

Think long-term. Act short-term.

Before you ask, “What should I do today?”

Ask yourself, “What should I remove today?”

Create the space you need to succeed.
How can I accomplish my goals as fast as possible at a high quality?
Am I willing to look foolish today so I can learn something that will make me better tomorrow?
What's one decision you can make today that will save you from making ten more decisions in the future? Make the choice that eliminates other choices.
When was the last time you felt a sense of wonder and awe? What can that experience teach you about how to spend your time?
What is a small, but courageous choice you can make today?

If someone took control of your life tomorrow, what’s the first thing they would change?

​
What is one of your natural gifts? How can you spend more time leveraging it?

Nearly everything in life has a useful zone, a desired dose. Ten minutes in the sun can energize you. Ten hours in the sun can burn you. This concept applies to many things: work, relationships, hobbies, exercise, food.

What is your desired dose? What do you need right now? A little bit more or a little bit less?
Write down all the projects you are working on right now. What is the one thing that, if you had the courage to eliminate it entirely, would make all the others easier?
Think of something you struggled with in the last year. If you step back and zoom out, what is one lesson you have learned from the experience?
There is usually a block of time each day when you are at your best—​peak energy, peak enthusiasm. Let's say it's 2 hours per day. How do you spend those 2 hours? Who or what gets your best time?
What is something wonderful about your life that you rarely appreciate as much as you should?

Entrepreneur and investor Sam Altman says some of the best advice he ever received was, “If you can't figure out what kind of work you like, pay attention to what's easy to concentrate on and gives you energy vs. what makes you tune out and feel tired.”

What is easy for you to concentrate on?

A question from Barrett Brooks on choosing your heroes:

“Here’s the thing about your heroes: You have to know about them to look up to them. The candidate pool is 100% limited by your exposure. That’s why so many kids look up to athletes, I think. They haven’t been exposed to enough other people to look up to them.

Here's how I think about that: Who haven’t I been exposed to that would inspire me if I knew they existed or knew the details of their lives? And how could I learn about those people?”
What is the most enjoyable five-minute stretch of your day? And how could you lengthen it to ten minutes?

A question from writer and programmer Simon Sarris:

If you know what you want, why are you waiting?
How can I make the next 60 seconds as perfect and as present as possible?

Habits need to be revised from time to time.

Which habits do you need to double down on this year? Which habits are no longer serving you and need to be replaced this year?
What is one lesson you learned (or relearned) this year?

What is something meaningful you can accomplish in the final week of the year?

The year isn't over yet. End on a high note.
What am I continuing to do out of habit, but is no longer serving me?
Are you playing a game worth winning?

A question from Paul Allen, the co-founder of Microsoft:

“What should exist? To me, that's the most exciting question imaginable. What do we need that we don't have?”
At this time next year, what will you be thankful you spent time on during the next 12 months?
What has been your favorite period of the last decade? How can you recreate some of that magic over the next year?
What is a small thing that bugs me, but I haven't taken the time to fix? Can I fix it today?

Look around the rooms where you spend the most time.

What behavior does this space encourage? How can you set things up to make your good habits easier?
What is the biggest non-work related contribution you can make today?
How much overlap is there between what you say is important to you and how you spent your attention over the last month?
How can today feel like play?
What if you stopped trying to think your way through it and started to act your way through it?
In what areas would you benefit from setting clearer boundaries?

To prioritize the day, think about the decade:

If I want to be on track to achieve X in 10 years, what do I need to do today?
Was this a productive week? What can you do today to guarantee the answer is yes?
What do you need to de-prioritize?

What's the cost of doing a poor job? What's the cost of doing a mediocre job? What's the cost of doing an exceptional job?

Which price are you willing to pay?
Which of my relationships are win-win? Which of my relationships are one-sided?
Six months from now, what you will you wish you had spent time on today?
What do I have planned for today that energizes me?

Thanks to Bryan Harris for sharing this week's question with me:

If it fails, where does it fail?

Faster. If I had to go from start to finish in half the time, what would I do?

Slower. If I could afford to spend double the time on it, what would I do?
Do I actually need more information or do I simply need to act on the information I already have?
What happens if I slow down? What happens if I speed up?

What is the most likely cause of failure?

Before it happens, how can I prevent it? If it happens, how can I recover?
What parts of my story no longer serve me? What stories am I attached to that I need to let go of?
People will tell stories about you at your funeral. What chapter are you writing today?
What is the limiting factor?
What is one action that would make today a success?
Do the people around me act the way I wish to act?
Am I working at the right level? Do I need to zoom in or zoom out?

A question from writer Elizabeth Gilbert:

“What do you love doing so much that the words failure and success essentially become irrelevant?”
What is a small pleasure that brings me great joy? Can I enjoy it today?

An insightful question from Steph Smith:

“How much of what you did today was simply due to inertia?

Never get so busy that you forget to actively design your life.”
How have my bad habits become a crutch I lean on? What stories do I need to let go of so I can walk freely?
If I keep doing what I am about to do today for the next five years, will I end up with more of what I want or less of what I want?
How can I create an environment that will naturally bring about my desired change?
What do I keep coming back to? What is that telling me?
How am I living with the results of other people's thinking?
Does the amount of time I’m giving this match its true importance?
What could be improved? What could be removed?

What 6-month period of your life was the most energizing and fun?

What can you learn from your answer?
What are my actions moving me closer to?

A question from venture capitalist and executive coach, Jerry Colonna:

“How are you complicit in creating the conditions you say you don’t want?”
What do I actually want?
Does this activity fill me with energy or drain me of energy?

Today's question comes from the engineer, Richard Hamming:

“If you do not work on important problems, how can you expect to do important work?”
What are you working on when time fades away?
Has the most important thing changed? Am I chasing an outdated target?

A simple question that can deliver powerful results if taken seriously:

What is the highest leverage action I can execute on right now?

If you met someone exactly like yourself …

– same experience– same resources– same problems

… what advice would you give them?
What is a mistake you seem to repeat each year? What can you do to prevent it this time?
What is best in the short-term? What is best in the long-term?
What is one small thing I could do today that would make a meaningful impact on my future?

Imagine the most important goal or project you are working on right now. Fast forward six months. Imagine the project has failed.

Why did you fail?

Here's a question that a reader shared with me:

Sometimes you have to pass through the fire. What fire or pain should you seek out in your life over the next year so you can learn its lessons?

Some questions to consider before you speak:

Does this need to be said?

Does this need to be said by me?

Does this need to be said by me right now?
What would your closest friend tell you to do?
What is one repeating problem you can automate or eliminate today?
What part of this situation is under my control?
Who can I collaborate with to make this easier?
What is the little bit of extra work that has huge upside?

Momentum is a double-edged sword. It can propel you to new heights or keep you locked into previous choices and old habits.

Where do I have healthy momentum right now? Where do I have unhealthy momentum?
What am I reinforcing each day?

This week, I'll steal a question from Richard Hamming's fabulous talk, You and Your Research.

What are the important problems in your field? And if you're not working on them, why not?
Who brings out your best qualities? Can you take five minutes right now to schedule time with them?

If you keep living the way you are, what will your life look like in 20 years?

Sometimes we need patience. Sometimes we need action.
Is there a better way? Is there a kinder way?
What are the 1-2 things that if you get them done today, you'll go to bed content?
What is one thing you can accomplish today that would make this day a success?
What is your personal compounding advantage in your career?
What am I holding on to that I need to let go of?
Am I being effective or just busy?
Which areas of my life are in maintenance mode? Which areas are in growth mode?
Imagine each day is only 12 hours long. What would you cut out?

Assume that more than one path exists to achieve your ideal life.

What would some of the alternative routes look like?
What am I avoiding just because the desired outcome would take longer than I'd like?
Am I being good to myself?
What can you work on today that will continue working for you years from now?
What are you preventing yourself from feeling?
Which of my current habits serves me most? Which serves me least?
What is the biggest small thing I could do today?
If someone could only see my actions and not hear my words, what would they say are my priorities?

Simple question to find work you love:

What do you enjoy refining? (It’s the areas you can’t help yourself from editing and optimizing where you have a long-term advantage.)
Am I doing this for Present Me or Future Me?
What is something that feels productive to you in the moment, but usually ends up wasting time and energy?

A simple question that may help reveal the positive side of the current moment:

What does this make possible?
Who do I know that can help me with this?
Am I proud of what I am choosing to do?
Can you sit still, do nothing, and breathe deeply for the next two minutes?
What is one thing I am looking forward to today?
Who is your biggest fan? How can you thank them today?

How can I make the most of this?

How would the person I wish to be act today?

This week's question builds on the quote from John Gardner above.

How are you collaborating in your defeat?

Don't take it the wrong way. This question doesn't mean your current situation is entirely your fault or even that it is 50/50. But the truth is you bring something into every interaction you will ever experience. (At the very least, you bring your attitude.)

How are you contributing to your own struggle?
The people who have already walked through the fire can help you do the same. Who are you surrounding yourself with?​
Do you really need to think more, or is it simply a matter of doing the work?
